notes.meaning: God gave this message to Ezekiel in the eleventh year of exile, just one month before the Babylonian army captured Jerusalem. At a moment when God's people were in deep distress, the Lord reminded them that the proud worldly empires around them would also face His justice.

The Lord tells Ezekiel to speak directly to Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, and to his huge army and noisy crowds. God opens with a challenge, asking Pharaoh if anyone on earth can match his immense power and majesty.

God tells Pharaoh to consider the fallen empire of Assyria, describing it as a magnificent cedar tree in Lebanon. It had thick, leafy branches that cast deep shade, and its top reached high into the clouds.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars propose translating the Hebrew word as 'tall cedar' or 'cypress' rather than the nation 'Assyria,' making the whole poem describe Egypt directly from the start.

notes.meaning: Plentiful underground springs and deep rivers nourished this cedar and helped it grow tall. The main stream watered the tree itself, while smaller canals ran out to nourish all the surrounding trees of the field.
Because it had such an endless supply of water, the tree towered far above all other trees. Its branches multiplied and stretched far and wide as it continued to grow.

The great cedar provided shelter for all kinds of life. Birds built nests in its branches, wild beasts birthed their young in its shade, and many powerful nations lived safely under its imperial protection.
The tree was magnificent in both height and breadth. Its roots reached deep into abundant waters, giving it stability, strength, and lasting health.
No tree in the garden of God could rival the splendor of this cedar. Even the finest cypresses and plane trees could not match its lush boughs or outshine its beauty.

The Lord makes it clear that He was the one who gave the tree its thick boughs and astonishing beauty. Its greatness was so dazzling that all the other trees in Eden, God's garden, looked on it with envy.
The Lord God explains why judgment had to fall. Because the tree grew so tall that its top touched the clouds, its heart became filled with pride and boastfulness over its own height.

Because of this wickedness, God handed the empire over to a mighty foreign ruler, King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon. The Lord drove the proud nation out from its position of honor just as He drove Adam from the garden.

Ruthless foreign soldiers cut down the mighty cedar and abandoned it on the ground. Its broken limbs lay scattered across mountains, valleys, and riverbeds, while the nations that once sheltered under it fled in fear.

The birds and beasts that once nested happily in the living tree now perched upon its ruined, fallen trunk. The image paints a picture of scavengers picking over a battlefield corpse after a terrible defeat.

God cut down this giant tree to give a warning to every other well-watered tree on earth. Earthly rulers and mighty nations must not become proud or rely on their own strength, because all human beings must eventually die and go down into the grave.

When the great king went down to the place of the dead, God caused deep grief across nature. The Lord closed up the underground springs, stopped the flowing rivers that made the tree great, and caused the forest of Lebanon to wither and faint in sadness.

The crash of the fallen empire made living nations shake with terror. Meanwhile, other kings and empires that had already died felt consoled in the realm of the dead, knowing that this arrogant superpower was brought just as low as they were.

All the allies, helper armies, and dependent nations that lived under Assyria's shadow were dragged down to death with it. Trusting in human military might cannot rescue anyone when God brings His judgment.

God turns the story directly onto Pharaoh, asking which magnificent tree of Eden he resembles. Just like Assyria, proud Egypt will be cast down to the grave to lie dishonored among the uncircumcised and those killed in war.
